title: Building PRISM: a self-reflection app for iPhone
summary: What PRISM is, the principles I am building it around, how its pieces fit together, and what I have and have not verified while it is in internal QA.
lead: PRISM is a bilingual iPhone app for self-reflection that I am building with a Flutter client and a FastAPI backend. It has a daily check-in, readings with a streamed AI reply, a private journal and a Self Map of patterns over time. It is in internal QA and has not been released. In this post I describe the product, the principles that shape the engineering, how the pieces fit together at a high level, and what I still have to prove before I would call it ready.

sections.title: What PRISM is
paragraphs: PRISM is meant to be a calm place to check in with how you feel, think something through and notice your own patterns. Each day has a short check-in with a card to reflect on. A reading starts from a question you choose, a spread and the cards you draw, and ends with a reply that explains each card in its position and suggests one small next step. A journal keeps notes and past readings, and a Self Map brings together a few ways of looking at yourself.

I use tarot as a mirror for reflection, not for prediction, and PRISM is not therapy. That positioning is a product decision with engineering consequences: replies must stay grounded in the cards and in what the person shared, and the app must behave carefully when someone writes something that sounds like distress.
The app is Vietnamese first and English from the start, so every string and every reply exists in both languages.

definitions.text: A short daily ritual: name how you feel, choose one small intention and read a card's reflection prompt.
A question, a spread of cards and a streamed reply that explains each card in its position.
A combined view of a few reflective lenses, such as numerology, birth cards and a personality test.
Private notes, check-ins and saved readings kept over time.

sections.title: Principles I am building around
paragraphs: Four principles drive most of the decisions, and I try to turn each into a check I can run.

Reflection, not prediction. Replies avoid dates, yes or no verdicts and claims about what other people think. This is easier to say than to enforce, so I treat it as something to evaluate on real Vietnamese and English cases.

Private by default. A journal is the most personal data in the app. I keep private text encrypted in storage and keep it out of logs and analytics, and I would rather debug from event types and request identifiers than from what someone wrote.
The server decides access. What is free, what needs a subscription and what a purchase unlocks is decided on the backend, so the app is a view of the account and not the authority on it.
Calm when things fail. A streamed reply can be cut off, a phone can go offline and a purchase can be delayed. I want each of those to end in a clear state the person understands, not in a spinner.

sections.title: How the pieces fit
paragraphs: The app is written in Flutter with Riverpod for state, and it queues journal changes offline so that a note written without a connection is not lost. The backend is a FastAPI modular monolith with async SQLAlchemy over PostgreSQL, which is the system of record. Redis supports rate limits and short-lived coordination, and a background worker handles scheduled maintenance.

Replies reach the app as a stream of text events over HTTP, so the first words appear while the rest is still being written. I chose a one-way stream because data only flows from the server to the app. The AI provider is selected by configuration, with separate settings for readings, chat and letters, and a built-in stand-in model lets every flow run locally without keys. Subscriptions and purchases go through a third-party subscription service.
I describe these pieces at a high level on purpose. The app is not released, and I do not want to publish the details of how access and usage are protected.

sections.title: What I have verified, and what I have not
paragraphs: The backend has an automated test suite that runs in continuous integration against a real database and cache, and the app has layout tests across phone sizes from small iPhones to wide displays. I have also reviewed screens in both languages on simulators. I did not rerun any of these for this post, and I treat passing tests as evidence about the code only.

What only real services can prove is still open. I have not yet completed the sandbox purchase and restore checks on real devices, a measured evaluation of reply quality in Vietnamese and English, or a review of how the whole system behaves with real subscribers. Until I have those results, I make no claims about cost, speed, quality or scale.

sections.title: What comes next
paragraphs: Next I want to finish the real-device purchase checks, run a larger evaluation of replies in both languages, including low-mood and prompt-injection cases, and measure how quickly the first words of a reply appear. When the app is on the App Store, I will link it here and write a follow-up with measured results.

takeaways: Turn product principles, such as reflection not prediction, into things you can test.
Keep private text encrypted and out of logs and analytics from the start.
Decide access on the server so the app only shows the account's state.
Design each failure, such as a cut-off reply or an offline note, to end in a clear state.
Say what is built, what is tested and what is still unproven while the app is unreleased.
